1. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science concerned with building machines and software
that can perform tasks that normally require human intelligence. These tasks include recognizing
patterns, understanding language, solving problems, making predictions, planning actions, and learning

from experience. AI systems use data, algorithms, and computing power to produce outputs that help
people make decisions or automate work.
The term artificial intelligence became widely used in academic research during the 1950s. Early
researchers explored whether computers could reason, solve puzzles, and use language. Modern AI has
expanded because digital data has become abundant, processors have become faster, and improved

expanded because digital data has become abundant, processors have become faster, and improved
algorithms can learn complex patterns. AI is now used in search engines, translation systems, navigation,
banking, education, agriculture, healthcare, manufacturing, and entertainment.
AI does not mean that a computer thinks or experiences the world exactly as a human does. Most
practical systems are designed for particular tasks. A program that detects spam may be excellent at

classifying email but cannot automatically diagnose a disease or drive a vehicle. Understanding this
distinction helps users evaluate what an AI system can and cannot do.
A typical AI application receives input, processes it using a model or set of rules, and produces an output.
For example, a speech assistant receives audio, converts it into text, interprets the request, selects an
action, and responds. The quality of the result depends on the data, model design, evaluation, and

action, and responds. The quality of the result depends on the data, model design, evaluation, and
operating environment.

2. Goals and Characteristics of AI
One important goal of AI is to help computers perform tasks that are difficult to describe using fixed
instructions. Traditional software follows rules written by a programmer. Machine-learning systems can
instead learn statistical patterns from examples. This makes them useful when the number of possible
situations is large or when the rules are hard to write explicitly.

situations is large or when the rules are hard to write explicitly.
AI systems commonly demonstrate abilities such as perception, reasoning, learning, language
processing, planning, and decision-making. Perception includes interpreting images, sound, and sensor
readings. Reasoning involves drawing conclusions from available information. Learning means improving
performance by identifying patterns in data. Planning selects a sequence of actions to reach a goal.

Automation is another major goal. An AI system can process repetitive information quickly and
consistently, allowing people to focus on tasks that require judgment, empathy, creativity, or
responsibility. AI can also support personalization by adapting recommendations, learning materials, or
interfaces to a person's needs.
Important characteristics of a useful AI system include accuracy, reliability, efficiency, adaptability,

explainability, and safety. These characteristics can conflict. A highly complex model may be accurate but
difficult to explain. A fast system may use fewer resources but make more errors. Developers therefore
choose designs based on the application's risks and requirements.
AI should be evaluated in the context in which it will be used. A small error rate may be acceptable for
suggesting music but unacceptable for identifying a critical medical condition. Good design begins by
defining the task, users, acceptable error levels, and consequences of failure.

3. Types of Artificial Intelligence
AI can be classified in several ways. A common introductory classification describes narrow AI, general
AI, and superintelligent AI. Narrow AI, also called weak AI, is designed to perform a specific task or a
limited set of related tasks. Examples include face detection, route planning, recommendation systems,
and voice transcription. Most AI applications available today belong to this category.

and voice transcription. Most AI applications available today belong to this category.
Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is a proposed form of AI that could learn and perform a broad range of
intellectual tasks at a flexible, human-like level. There is no universally accepted test for AGI, and current
systems should not be assumed to possess it. Research continues into more general capabilities, but
claims about AGI require careful definitions and evidence.

claims about AGI require careful definitions and evidence.
Artificial Superintelligence is a hypothetical system whose intellectual abilities would exceed those of
humans across many important domains. It is a subject of debate in AI research, ethics, and policy rather
than a description of ordinary products.
Another classification considers how systems operate. Reactive systems respond to current inputs

Another classification considers how systems operate. Reactive systems respond to current inputs
without maintaining a meaningful internal record of past events. Limited-memory systems use recent or
stored information to improve decisions. More complex categories, such as systems that understand
beliefs or possess self-awareness, are often discussed as theoretical concepts.
These classifications are useful for explaining different ambitions and capabilities, but they do not by

themselves measure quality. A narrow system can be extremely valuable when it performs a well-defined
task accurately and safely.

4. History and Development of AI
The development of AI has taken place over many decades. In the 1940s and 1950s, researchers
developed mathematical models of computation and began asking whether machines could demonstrate
intelligent behavior. The 1956 Dartmouth research workshop is commonly associated with the
establishment of artificial intelligence as a named field.

establishment of artificial intelligence as a named field.
Early AI programs solved puzzles, played simple games, and manipulated symbols. Researchers
believed that reasoning could be represented through formal rules. However, limited computing power,
small datasets, and the difficulty of real-world language and perception restricted progress. Periods of
reduced funding and expectations became known as AI winters.

reduced funding and expectations became known as AI winters.
Expert systems became prominent in the 1970s and 1980s. These programs used knowledge bases and
hand-written rules to provide advice in narrow domains. They demonstrated that computers could support
specialized decisions, but they were expensive to maintain and struggled when situations differed from
their programmed rules.
From the 1990s onward, statistical machine learning became increasingly important. Instead of writing

every rule, developers trained models using examples. Larger datasets, improved hardware, and deep
learning led to major advances in image recognition, speech processing, and language technology during
the 2010s.
Transformer architectures, introduced in 2017, helped accelerate progress in language models.
Generative AI systems can now produce text, images, audio, and code. The history of AI shows that
progress depends not only on algorithms but also on data, computing resources, evaluation, and

progress depends not only on algorithms but also on data, computing resources, evaluation, and
responsible deployment.

5. Machine Learning
Machine learning (ML) is a major area of AI in which computer systems learn patterns from data and use
those patterns to make predictions or decisions. Rather than receiving every rule directly from a
programmer, a model is trained using examples. The model adjusts internal parameters to reduce errors
on a defined learning task.

on a defined learning task.
Supervised learning uses labelled examples. Each training example contains input data and a known
target, such as an image labelled as a cat or a house record paired with its sale price. Classification
predicts a category, while regression predicts a numerical value. Examples include spam detection,
disease-risk estimation, and demand forecasting.
Unsupervised learning works with data that has no supplied target labels. It can discover groups,

Unsupervised learning works with data that has no supplied target labels. It can discover groups,
patterns, or compact representations. Clustering groups similar customers, while dimensionality reduction
represents data using fewer variables. These methods can help explore large datasets.
Reinforcement learning trains an agent through interaction with an environment. The agent takes actions

and receives rewards or penalties. Over time it learns a policy that aims to maximize long-term reward. It
is used in research on robotics, game-playing, and resource allocation.
A machine-learning workflow includes defining the problem, collecting data, cleaning and preparing it,
selecting a model, training, validating, testing, and monitoring. Data leakage, biased samples, and
overfitting can make a model appear successful during development but fail in real use. A separate test
set and ongoing monitoring help estimate real-world performance.

6. Deep Learning and Neural Networks
Deep learning is a branch of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. These
networks are inspired loosely by the connected structure of biological neurons, although artificial neurons
are mathematical functions rather than realistic brain cells. Each layer transforms its input and passes the
result to the next layer.

result to the next layer.
An artificial neuron receives numerical inputs, multiplies them by weights, adds a bias, and applies an
activation function. During training, the network compares its prediction with the expected answer. A loss
function measures the error, and an optimization method updates the weights to reduce that error.
Backpropagation calculates how changes in weights affect the loss.

Backpropagation calculates how changes in weights affect the loss.
Deep networks can learn useful representations from raw or lightly processed data. In image recognition,
early layers may respond to edges and textures, while later layers may represent object parts and
complete objects. In language tasks, networks learn relationships among words and pieces of words from
large collections of text.
Deep learning has achieved strong results in computer vision, speech recognition, natural language

Deep learning has achieved strong results in computer vision, speech recognition, natural language
processing, and scientific applications. However, it often requires substantial data and computing
resources. Large models can be difficult to interpret and may reproduce patterns or biases present in their
training data.
A neural network is not automatically appropriate for every problem. For a small structured dataset, a

simpler model may be faster, easier to explain, and just as accurate. Model choice should be guided by
evidence and practical constraints.

7. Natural Language Processing
Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the area of AI that enables computers to work with human
language. Language is complex because words can have multiple meanings, grammar varies, and
meaning depends on context, culture, and situation. NLP combines computational linguistics, machine
learning, and language modelling to process text and speech.

learning, and language modelling to process text and speech.
Common NLP tasks include tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, named-entity recognition, sentiment
analysis, translation, summarization, question answering, and text classification. Tokenization divides text
into smaller units such as words, subwords, or punctuation. Named-entity recognition identifies items
such as people, organizations, dates, and locations.

such as people, organizations, dates, and locations.
Sentiment analysis estimates whether text expresses a positive, negative, or neutral attitude. Machine
translation converts text from one language to another. Text summarization produces a shorter version
that preserves important information. Search systems use language processing to match a query with
relevant documents.
NLP systems may use rule-based methods, statistical models, neural networks, or combinations of these

approaches. Modern language models learn patterns from large text collections and can perform multiple
tasks through instructions or examples.
Evaluation must consider more than grammatical fluency. A response may sound natural but contain
incorrect facts. NLP applications should be tested for accuracy, fairness across languages and dialects,
privacy, and robustness to misspellings or unusual phrasing.

8. Computer Vision
Computer vision is the field of AI that enables computers to interpret visual information from images and
videos. A computer vision system may identify objects, locate people, classify scenes, read text, estimate
movement, or inspect products for defects. Cameras and other sensors provide the visual input.
Image classification assigns a label to an entire image. Object detection identifies objects and estimates

their locations, often using bounding boxes. Image segmentation assigns labels to individual pixels or
regions. Facial analysis may detect a face or estimate visible landmarks; the use of such systems
requires particular attention to consent, privacy, and fairness.
Deep convolutional neural networks were widely used for image tasks because they can learn spatial
patterns such as edges, shapes, and textures. Vision transformers and other architectures have also

patterns such as edges, shapes, and textures. Vision transformers and other architectures have also
become important. Training usually requires labelled images or other learning signals, along with careful
evaluation on data that represents real deployment conditions.
Applications include medical image support, quality inspection in factories, crop monitoring, traffic
analysis, accessibility tools, and document scanning. In agriculture, vision models can help identify visible

signs of plant disease. In manufacturing, cameras can detect surface defects more consistently than
manual inspection in some settings.
Lighting, camera angle, image quality, occlusion, and changes in the environment can affect
performance. A system should be tested under realistic conditions and should not be trusted as the sole
decision-maker in high-impact situations without suitable safeguards.

9. Generative Artificial Intelligence
Generative AI refers to systems that create new content based on patterns learned from training data.
The output may be text, images, audio, video, computer code, or structured information. Unlike a system
that only classifies an input, a generative model produces a new sequence or representation.

that only classifies an input, a generative model produces a new sequence or representation.
Large language models generate text by estimating likely next tokens based on the preceding context.
Image-generation models may learn to transform noise into images that match a text description. Audio
models can generate speech, music, or sound effects. Different model families use different training
objectives and architectures.

objectives and architectures.
Generative AI can support brainstorming, drafting, tutoring, translation, coding assistance, and creative
exploration. It can help users produce a first draft quickly, but the result should be reviewed. Models can
generate inaccurate statements, fabricated references, outdated information, or code containing errors.
This behavior is sometimes called hallucination.
The quality of an output depends on the prompt, model, context, and task. Clear instructions, relevant

source material, and examples can improve results. Users should avoid entering confidential information
unless the service and its data-handling terms are appropriate.
Responsible use includes checking factual claims, respecting copyright and privacy, identifying synthetic
media where relevant, and keeping humans accountable for important decisions. Generative AI is best
treated as an assistant rather than an unquestionable authority.

10. Transformers and Attention
The Transformer is a neural network architecture that has become central to modern language modelling.
It was introduced in the 2017 research paper titled “Attention Is All You Need.” Transformers use attention
mechanisms to relate different parts of an input sequence and can process many tokens in parallel during
training.

training.
Self-attention allows each token to calculate how strongly it should use information from other tokens.
The model creates query, key, and value representations. Similarity between a query and keys produces
attention scores. After normalization, these scores weight the value vectors, creating a context-aware
representation.
Multi-head attention performs several attention calculations in parallel. Different heads can learn different

relationships, such as nearby grammatical connections or longer-range dependencies. Positional
information is added because attention alone does not inherently represent the order of tokens.
A Transformer commonly contains attention layers, feed-forward networks, residual connections, and
normalization. Encoder-only models are often used for understanding tasks, decoder-only models for text
generation, and encoder-decoder models for tasks such as translation.

generation, and encoder-decoder models for tasks such as translation.
Transformers can model long-range relationships effectively, but their computational and memory
requirements can grow substantially with sequence length. Researchers continue to develop more
efficient attention methods and architectures. Understanding attention helps explain why modern
language models can use context, although attention weights should not be interpreted as a complete
explanation of a model's reasoning.

11. Large Language Models
A Large Language Model (LLM) is a model trained on large amounts of text to learn statistical patterns in
language. Many LLMs use Transformer architectures. Text is divided into tokens, and the model learns to
predict or otherwise represent token sequences. Training adjusts a large number of parameters using
examples.

examples.
After pretraining, a model may be adapted for instruction following, conversation, coding, or specialized
tasks. Fine-tuning uses additional examples to adjust model behavior. Preference-based training can
further encourage responses that people judge more useful or appropriate. Different systems use
different combinations of these methods.
An LLM can summarize text, answer questions, translate, classify, draft documents, and generate code.

Its broad abilities come from patterns learned during training and the context supplied at use time. It does
not automatically have access to current events, private databases, or the internet unless tools or
connected sources provide that access.
LLMs have limitations. They may confidently produce incorrect information, misunderstand ambiguous
instructions, struggle with precise calculations, or reflect biases in data. Their context window also limits

how much information they can consider at once.
Good use involves supplying relevant context, asking focused questions, checking important claims
against reliable sources, and protecting sensitive data. In professional settings, organizations should
evaluate models on representative tasks before deployment.

12. Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a system design that combines information retrieval with
generative AI. Instead of asking a language model to answer only from its learned parameters, a RAG
system first searches an external collection for relevant information. It then provides the retrieved material
to the model as context for generating an answer.

to the model as context for generating an answer.
A typical RAG pipeline has several stages. Documents are loaded from sources such as PDFs, web
pages, or text files. The text is cleaned and divided into chunks. An embedding model converts each
chunk into a numerical vector. These vectors and their associated text are stored in a vector database.
When a user asks a question, the system embeds the query and searches for nearby document vectors.

When a user asks a question, the system embeds the query and searches for nearby document vectors.
It retrieves the most relevant chunks and places them into a prompt with instructions. The language
model generates an answer using the supplied context. The system can also show the retrieved
passages so users can verify the response.
RAG is useful for company policies, manuals, course notes, technical documentation, and other

RAG is useful for company policies, manuals, course notes, technical documentation, and other
collections that change more often than a model can be retrained. It can make answers more grounded in
a selected knowledge base, but it does not guarantee correctness. Poor retrieval, missing documents,
misleading text, or weak prompts can still lead to errors.
A good RAG system evaluates retrieval quality and answer quality separately. It should preserve

A good RAG system evaluates retrieval quality and answer quality separately. It should preserve
document references, handle questions with no supporting evidence, and avoid inventing information
when the source material does not contain an answer.

13. Text Extraction and Chunking
Document processing is an important first stage in a PDF question-answering system. A PDF may
contain paragraphs, headings, tables, page numbers, images, and footnotes. A text-extraction library can
retrieve selectable text, but complex layouts may produce text in an unexpected order. Scanned PDFs
may require optical character recognition (OCR).

may require optical character recognition (OCR).
After extraction, the text is usually divided into smaller sections called chunks. Chunking makes retrieval
more focused and helps fit source material into a language model's context window. A chunk may contain
a paragraph, a fixed number of characters, or a certain number of tokens.
Chunk size affects retrieval. Very small chunks may omit important context, while very large chunks may

contain unrelated information and make matching less precise. Overlap preserves some text between
adjacent chunks so that a fact split across a boundary is less likely to be lost.
For example, a document can be split into chunks of 500 characters with an overlap of 100 characters.
These are experimental settings rather than universal best values. A useful project compares multiple
sizes and overlap values using the same set of questions.

sizes and overlap values using the same set of questions.
Each chunk should retain metadata such as its source filename, page number, and chunk identifier.
Metadata makes it easier to trace a generated answer back to the original document. Before embedding,
remove unnecessary repeated headers and check for extraction errors, but preserve meaningful
headings and section context.

14. Embeddings and Vector Databases
An embedding is a numerical representation of data, such as a sentence or paragraph. Embedding
models map text into vectors so that pieces of text with related meanings can be placed near each other
in a mathematical space. The vector contains many numerical dimensions, and each dimension
contributes to the representation learned by the model.

contributes to the representation learned by the model.
Semantic search uses embeddings to find meaning-related content rather than relying only on exact word
matches. For example, a query asking “How can machines learn from examples?” may retrieve a
passage about machine learning even if the exact phrase does not appear.
Similarity can be measured in different ways. Cosine similarity compares the direction of two vectors. Dot

product measures their inner product, and Euclidean distance measures straight-line distance. The
correct interpretation depends on the embedding model and the vector database's configuration. A
similarity score is a ranking signal, not automatically a probability that an answer is correct.
A vector database stores embeddings and supports efficient similarity search. ChromaDB is one option. A
collection can store each vector alongside its text and metadata. When a query arrives, the database

finds nearby vectors and returns the corresponding records.
The quality of semantic search depends on the embedding model, chunking strategy, query wording, and
source content. Developers should inspect retrieved passages and evaluate results with realistic
questions instead of assuming that the highest score always represents a correct answer.

15. Semantic Search and Keyword Search
Keyword-based search finds documents by matching words or terms in a query. A simple approach
counts matching terms. More advanced traditional methods include TF-IDF and BM25, which consider
term frequency and how common a word is across a document collection. These methods can be
effective when users know the exact terminology.

effective when users know the exact terminology.
Semantic search attempts to match meaning. It commonly uses embeddings to represent queries and
documents as vectors, then ranks documents by vector similarity. It may retrieve a relevant passage even
when the query uses synonyms or different wording from the document.
For example, a document might say “neural networks improve through training,” while a user asks “How

do artificial neurons get better?” Keyword search may find fewer direct matches. Semantic search may
recognize that the question is conceptually related to model training.
Neither method is always superior. Keyword search can perform well for product codes, names, exact
phrases, legal references, and technical identifiers. Semantic search can help with natural-language
questions and paraphrases. Semantic methods may miss exact rare terms, while keyword methods may

questions and paraphrases. Semantic methods may miss exact rare terms, while keyword methods may
return passages that share words but not meaning.
Hybrid search combines lexical and semantic signals. A system may retrieve candidates using both
methods and combine their rankings. Evaluation should compare methods on the same queries,
document collection, and Top-5 limit. Useful measures include relevance judgments, precision at five,
recall, and inspection of similarity or ranking scores.

16. ChromaDB in a RAG Application
ChromaDB is an open-source vector database that can store embeddings and associated records for
similarity search. In a RAG project, each record typically includes a unique identifier, the original text
chunk, an embedding vector, and metadata. Metadata may include a filename, page number, or section
heading.

heading.
A collection groups related records. For example, a collection named “ai_pdf_collection” can contain
chunks extracted from an Artificial Intelligence PDF. Keeping collections organized helps separate
different document sets and prevents accidental mixing of unrelated sources.
A typical workflow creates or opens a persistent ChromaDB client, creates a collection, and adds
documents with identifiers and metadata. The embedding model converts the text into vectors. At query

time, the query is embedded and compared with stored vectors. The database returns the nearest
records according to its configured distance metric.
Persistent storage is useful because the system does not need to rebuild the database every time the
application starts. The database directory should be treated as project data and should not be confused
with source code. If the embedding model or chunking strategy changes, rebuilding the collection may be
necessary.

necessary.
Developers should avoid duplicate identifiers, keep metadata consistent, and verify that the collection
contains the expected number of chunks. Search results should be checked against the original PDF to
ensure that extraction and indexing have preserved the intended content.

17. Ollama and Local Language Models
Ollama is a tool for running supported language models locally on a computer. It provides a way to
download models, start a local service, and send prompts to a model without relying on a hosted
language-model API for each request. Local inference can be useful for learning, prototyping, and
applications where data should remain within a controlled environment.

applications where data should remain within a controlled environment.
A model is selected based on its capabilities, size, memory requirements, and the computer's hardware.
Smaller models may run on ordinary computers but can produce less detailed responses. Larger models
may provide stronger results but require more memory and processing power. Performance also depends
on quantization, CPU or GPU support, and other runtime settings.

on quantization, CPU or GPU support, and other runtime settings.
In a RAG application, Ollama receives a prompt containing the user's question and the retrieved
document chunks. The prompt should instruct the model to answer only from the supplied context. If the
context does not contain the answer, the model should say that the information is unavailable in the
document.
Running a model locally does not remove every security or privacy risk. Files, logs, plugins, and network

settings still need appropriate protection. Users should understand where model files are stored and
which services can access the machine.
A local model should be tested with questions whose answers are known from the PDF. Compare its
response with the source text and record cases where it omits details, misinterprets a passage, or
introduces unsupported claims.

18. Evaluating a PDF Question-Answering System
Evaluation determines whether a PDF question-answering system retrieves useful evidence and
generates accurate answers. These are related but separate tasks. Retrieval evaluation asks whether
relevant chunks appear among the results. Generation evaluation asks whether the final answer is
supported, complete, and understandable.

supported, complete, and understandable.
A practical evaluation set should contain questions with answers distributed across the PDF. Include
direct questions, paraphrased questions, questions about definitions, and questions that require
combining information from more than one passage. Include at least a few questions whose answers are
not present in the document to test whether the system can admit uncertainty.

not present in the document to test whether the system can admit uncertainty.
For retrieval, inspect the Top-5 chunks for each query. Precision at five measures the fraction of the five
retrieved chunks that are relevant, while recall measures how much of the known relevant material was
retrieved. If no human relevance labels are available, manually review a sample and record the judgment
criteria.
For answer quality, compare the generated response with the source evidence. Check factual

For answer quality, compare the generated response with the source evidence. Check factual
correctness, coverage of key points, clarity, and whether unsupported claims appear. Similarity scores
help rank candidates, but they do not replace human review.
Record questions, retrieved chunk IDs, source pages, scores, generated answers, and observations in
CSV files. This makes the experiment reproducible and helps identify whether poor answers result from
extraction, chunking, retrieval, or generation.

19. Applications, Benefits, and Challenges of AI
AI is used across many sectors. In healthcare, it can assist with image analysis, administrative work, and
research, while clinical decisions remain subject to professional oversight. In education, AI can support
tutoring, language practice, feedback, and accessible learning materials. In agriculture, predictive tools

and image analysis can support crop monitoring and resource planning.
Businesses use AI for demand forecasting, customer support, fraud detection, document processing, and
quality inspection. Transport systems use AI-related methods for route planning, traffic prediction, and
driver assistance. Scientific researchers use machine learning to analyze large datasets and identify
patterns that may be difficult to detect manually.

patterns that may be difficult to detect manually.
Potential benefits include faster processing, improved consistency, personalization, support for complex
analysis, and wider access to digital tools. AI can also create new risks. Models may be biased,
inaccurate, insecure, difficult to explain, or expensive to operate. Automation can change job tasks and
require workers to develop new skills.
Responsible adoption begins with a clear purpose and an assessment of who may be affected.

Responsible adoption begins with a clear purpose and an assessment of who may be affected.
Organizations should test systems on representative data, monitor performance, protect personal
information, provide human review for high-impact decisions, and create ways to report problems.
AI should complement human expertise rather than remove accountability. The appropriate level of
automation depends on the consequences of error, the quality of available evidence, and the needs and
rights of affected people.

20. Future of AI and Conclusion
AI research is likely to continue advancing in multimodal systems, efficient models, robotics, scientific
discovery, and tools that can use external software. Multimodal AI works with more than one kind of input,
such as text, images, audio, and video. These systems may support more natural interfaces and help
people analyze complex information.

people analyze complex information.
Another important direction is efficiency. Researchers are developing smaller models, improved
hardware, compression methods, and techniques that reduce the energy and computing resources
required for training and inference. Specialized models may be more suitable than very large general
models for some applications.
Trustworthy AI will remain essential. Future systems need stronger evaluation, privacy protection,

Trustworthy AI will remain essential. Future systems need stronger evaluation, privacy protection,
security, transparency, fairness, and mechanisms for human oversight. Laws, standards, and
organizational policies will influence how AI is designed and deployed. Technical performance alone is
not enough to establish that a system is appropriate.
This guide has introduced the foundations of AI, machine learning, deep learning, NLP, computer vision,

generative AI, Transformers, LLMs, RAG, embeddings, vector databases, semantic search, and local
inference. These concepts work together in a PDF question-answering application: the document is
extracted, divided into chunks, embedded, indexed, searched, and passed to a language model as
evidence.
A successful AI project combines sound technical design with careful testing and responsible use. By
comparing semantic and keyword search, recording similarity scores, and checking generated answers

comparing semantic and keyword search, recording similarity scores, and checking generated answers
against the original PDF, students can understand both the strengths and limitations of modern
information-retrieval systems.
